Limits, caching and replay

Source: vignettes/runs.Rmd
runs.Rmd

Every stage of harnessr except one is a pure function of its input. Extraction, cleaning, segmentation, ranking and merging give the same result every time. The model call is the exception. It is the only step that costs money and the only one that can die halfway through a long run. Above a temperature of zero, it is also the only step whose reply can differ from one call to the next.

This guide covers how harnessr handles that step: the record each run keeps, the limits every request is checked against before it is sent, a cache that makes a repeat free, and a replay that reproduces a run from its trace with no key and no spend. harnessr ships no model prices: “Prices” in vignette("models") shows how to set the prices you pay and keep them current, with the model registry and token counts. How much a reasoning model reasons, and effort that rises only when a stage needs it (effort_mode), are in vignette("effort"). vignette("harnessr") introduces the package and its ideas.

Setting up

The examples run offline. hr_mock_client() plays the part of the model, and embedder = "lexical" gives free, deterministic word-overlap vectors in place of an embeddings endpoint.

A mock costs nothing, so the spending limits below would have nothing to count. The examples give it a price instead. hr_register_model() registers the model id "priced-mock" at $2 per million input tokens and $8 per million output tokens. Runs that name that model are priced at those rates, and most runs below do.

library(harnessr)

# Illustrative prices for a stand-in model. For a real model, use your
# provider's current prices.
hr_register_model("priced-mock", context_window = 128000, max_output = 4096,
                  input_usd = 2, output_usd = 8)
old <- hr_options(verbose = FALSE, embedder = "lexical")

cl <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.")

What a run records

The answer carries everything in this section, and print(ans) sums it up: the cost, where the evidence came from and, for a partial answer, why.

ans <- answer_document(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", "thorough",
                       client = cl, model = "priced-mock", max_tokens = 150)
ans
#> <gr_answer> reader=map_reduce
#>   Q: What was revenue?
#>   11 model call(s), 2444 in / 143 out tokens, 0 error(s), $0.0060 across priced-mock, prices as of 2026-11
#>   ---
#> Revenue was 45.2 million dollars. 
#>   ---
#>   Evidence: chunk 1, chunk 2, chunk 3 ("Operations"), chunk 4, chunk 5, chunk 6, and 4 more

Check ans$partial first. TRUE means something degraded, and ans$notes lists what: dropped_chunks, failed_calls, unread_pages, call_cap_reached, cost_cap_reached and so on. ans$warnings holds every warning raised while the document was read.

The trace holds every request the run made. hr_trace_summary() gives the totals, hr_trace_cost() the bill by model, and as.data.frame() one row per request with its stage, tokens, cost, time, prompt and reply:

hr_trace_summary(ans$trace)[, c("calls", "cached", "tokens_in", "tokens_out", "errors")]
#>   calls cached tokens_in tokens_out errors
#> 1    11      0      2444        143      0
hr_trace_cost(ans$trace)[, c("model", "calls", "paid_calls", "usd", "priced", "as_of")]
#>         model calls paid_calls      usd priced   as_of
#> 1 priced-mock    11         11 0.006032   TRUE 2026-11
as.data.frame(ans$trace)[, c("step", "stage", "tokens_in", "tokens_out", "usd")]
#>    step      stage tokens_in tokens_out      usd
#> 1     4 map.answer       204         13 0.000512
#> 2     5 map.answer       210         13 0.000524
#> 3     6 map.answer       227         13 0.000558
#> 4     7 map.answer       179         13 0.000462
#> 5     8 map.answer       221         13 0.000546
#> 6     9 map.answer       221         13 0.000546
#> 7    10 map.answer       228         13 0.000560
#> 8    11 map.answer       226         13 0.000556
#> 9    12 map.answer       205         13 0.000514
#> 10   13 map.answer       227         13 0.000558
#> 11   14     reduce       296         13 0.000696

The token totals measure the prompts and replies, so they show the size of a run. The bill comes from hr_trace_cost(), which counts only the calls that were issued. A call answered from a cache or a recording spent nothing, however long its prompt. A model with no registered price contributes NA, never 0, so no total can leave one out unnoticed.

Each row also says where its price came from: priced (whether the model has a price), as_of (the month of that price) and certain (FALSE when the registry only guessed the model from its name). Every report of a cost in dollars carries the same three columns, and a printed cost gives the month, as in “prices as of 2026-11”. For a model with no price it prints “no price set for” the model and names hr_register_model() and hr_load_models(). A total over several models, some without a price, says it covers the priced models only.

hr_estimate_cost() prices a run before you make it:

hr_estimate_cost("priced-mock", input_tokens = 120000, output_tokens = 4000)
#> [1] 0.272

With detail = TRUE it returns the figure with the same three columns:

hr_estimate_cost("priced-mock", 120000, 4000, detail = TRUE)
#>         model   usd priced   as_of certain
#> 1 priced-mock 0.272   TRUE 2026-11    TRUE

What each request records

Each request is one entry in trace$steps. Besides its label, prompt, reply and the model requested, a step records:

  • params, what the call asked for, and params_sent, the request as it went out with every default resolved: the model, api, base_url, the output cap sent, the temperature (NA when none was sent), the effort, the schema name, and SHA-256 hashes of the JSON schema and of any extra body fields. A small cap sent to a reasoning model is raised to 2048, and params_sent shows the raised cap.
  • served_model, response_id and fingerprint, where the provider returns them. model keeps the model requested, and the step is priced and replayed by that model.
  • attempts, the number of requests sent, retries included (0 for a reply from a cache or a recording), and started_utc and ended_utc in ISO 8601 UTC.
  • tokens, with provenance: "reported" by the provider, "counted" here with the "tiktoken" tokenizer, or "estimated" with another one. Reasoning and cached input tokens the provider reports are kept as tokens$reasoning and tokens$cached_input, as parts of output and input rather than additions.
step <- ans$trace$steps[[length(ans$trace$steps)]]
str(step[c("label", "attempts", "started_utc", "tokens")])
#> List of 4
#>  $ label      : chr "reduce"
#>  $ attempts   : int 1
#>  $ started_utc: chr "2026-11-27T17:46:06.331Z"
#>  $ tokens     :List of 3
#>   ..$ input     : int 296
#>   ..$ output    : int 13
#>   ..$ provenance: chr "estimated"
str(step$params_sent)
#> List of 9
#>  $ model          : chr "priced-mock"
#>  $ api            : chr "mock"
#>  $ base_url       : chr "mock://"
#>  $ max_output     : int 1500
#>  $ temperature    : num NA
#>  $ effort         : chr NA
#>  $ schema_name    : chr NA
#>  $ schema_hash    : chr NA
#>  $ extra_body_hash: chr NA

A mock reports no usage, so its counts are estimated. hr_trace_summary() gives the share of requests whose counts were estimated as usage_estimated, and print() on a trace reports that share when it is above zero.

refine and hierarchical also record the length of the state they carry forward:

  • Each refine.draft and refine.revise step has state$tokens_in, the length of the draft the request carried, and state$tokens_out, the length of the draft carried on from it (the old draft when the reply was unusable).
  • Each hier.summarise.L<k> step has the length of the text it summarised and of the summary it returned.
  • Each level adds a local hier.state.L<k> step with the number of summaries handed on and their combined length.

A draft that shrinks sharply in one revision shows up in these fields.

Each cut made to fit a limit writes a local truncate step. It holds where the cut was made (detail$where), the token limit, and the tokens before, kept and dropped. A refine or hierarchical answer also adds up the tokens cut in notes$tokens_truncated, and printing the answer reports how many tokens were cut to fit. Here a model with a 1,000-token window makes refine cut its growing draft:

hr_register_model("small-window", context_window = 1000, max_output = 500,
                  input_usd = 2, output_usd = 8)
long_draft <- paste(rep("Revenue was 45.2 million dollars, and the draft says so.", 30),
                    collapse = " ")
cut <- answer_document(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", "fast",
                       client = hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) long_draft),
                       reader = "refine", model = "small-window",
                       max_tokens = 120, max_answer_tokens = 200)
cuts <- Filter(function(s) identical(s$label, "truncate"), cut$trace$steps)
str(cuts[[1]]$detail)
#> List of 6
#>  $ where         : chr "refine.draft"
#>  $ limit         : int 280
#>  $ tokens_before : int 453
#>  $ tokens_kept   : int 271
#>  $ tokens_dropped: int 182
#>  $ chunk_id      : int 2
cut$notes$tokens_truncated
#> [1] 910

A cut can also be made at refine.excerpt, refine.ledger, hier.summaries, preview.skim, preview.outline, <label>.input for a finding cut to fit a merge, <label>.giveup for the capped findings a failed merge returns, segment.contextual.header, segment.contextual.document, screen.opening, synthesise.gaps and embed.input.

A trace also records who the run is for and the settings it ran under. hr_trace() takes system, owner, run_by, purpose and approved_by. hr_options(actor = list(...)) sets them for every trace, and a field you set in neither place is NA. trace$config is a snapshot of the options in force when the trace was made, plus the R version. It leaves out the values of api_headers, since they can hold credentials.

tr <- hr_trace(owner = "finance team", run_by = "ana", purpose = "Q3 check")
tr
#> <gr_trace run_20261127174606.653_1de347>  0 steps, 0 model calls, 0 in / 0 out tokens, 0 error(s)
#>   cost: no cost recorded
#>   actor: owner = finance team, run_by = ana, purpose = Q3 check 
#>   started: 2026-11-27T17:46:06.653Z
names(tr$config)
#> [1] "options"   "r_version"

as_json(ans) writes the answer with every prompt and response of its run. hr_trace_save() writes the trace alone, and a replay reads that file.

Errors and warnings by class

Errors are classed, so you can catch a specific failure:

  • gr_auth_error, gr_file_not_found, gr_empty_document, gr_unsupported_format, gr_overflow, gr_call_cap, gr_cost_cap, gr_budget_error, gr_unknown_model, gr_unknown_override, gr_no_recipes, gr_bad_ensemble and gr_missing_dep.
  • gr_bad_setting for a setting outside its choices (vignette("core")).
  • hr_unknown_effort_key (vignette("effort")), and hr_unpriced_model when allow_unpriced = FALSE refuses a model with no price.
  • hr_dim_mismatch when two vectors of different lengths are compared, such as a lexical fallback vector against an API embedding.

Degradations are classed warnings:

  • gr_segment_fallback, gr_embed_fallback, gr_rerank_degraded, gr_iterative_degraded, gr_ensemble_degenerate, gr_duplicate_recipe and gr_ocr_unavailable.
  • gr_clamped with hr_param_clamped for a parameter moved to its nearest bound (vignette("core")).
  • gr_parallel_share for a parallel item whose share refused a later request (below).
  • gr_bad_correct for a gr_compare() correct function that fails (below).
  • gr_unclear_dropped when gr_extract() leaves unclear screening records out (vignette("review")).
  • hr_unpriced_model for a request sent to a model with no price under a spending limit, and hr_stale_price for a cost computed from old prices, each once per model per session (below).

In an interactive session, a long read keeps one progress line up to date with the number of chunks read and the spend so far. gr_read_many() also reports the spend so far before each document.

Limits

Two limits are on by default: a run may spend $5 and make 400 calls.

unlist(hr_options()[c("max_cost_usd", "max_calls")])
#> max_cost_usd    max_calls 
#>            5          400

They are checked at two points. Before the first request, a run is refused, with a classed error that names the option to change, when:

  • it would need more calls than max_calls, or
  • its reader sends every chunk, and sending them would already cost more than max_cost_usd.

Here map_reduce over five chunks needs six calls:

chunks <- gr_segment(gr_example(), list(method = "sentence", max_tokens = 150))
spec <- gr_read_spec(reader = "map_reduce", model = "priced-mock")

tryCatch(
  gr_read(chunks, "What was revenue?", cl, spec,
          trace = hr_trace(governor = hr_governor(max_calls = 3))),
  gr_call_cap = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
#> [1] "Reader 'map_reduce' over 5 chunks would need about 6 more model calls (0 already made this run), above the 3-call cap. Use a larger `max_tokens` when segmenting (fewer chunks), pick a top-k reader, or raise hr_options(max_calls = ...)."

Every request is checked before it is sent

The second check runs on every request before it goes out. It compares the limit with what the run has spent plus the most the request could cost: its prompt at the input price and its output cap at the output price. The prompt count includes the JSON schema and extra body fields the request carries and a few tokens of framing per message, since the provider bills for all of that. That count is then raised by safety_margin. A request that could take the run past a limit is not sent, so a run ends at or under its limit rather than one request over it.

Under a limit of one cent, the five chunk requests below go out and the merge does not. The merge’s reply cap is 1500 tokens, which at $8 per million could cost more than the run has left, so the answer comes back partial:

tr <- hr_trace(governor = hr_governor(max_cost_usd = 0.01))
capped <- gr_read(chunks, "What was revenue?", cl, spec, trace = tr)
capped$partial
#> [1] TRUE
data.frame(calls = tr$calls, spent_usd = tr$spent_usd, stop_reason = tr$stop_reason)
#>   calls spent_usd stop_reason
#> 1     5  0.002428        cost
tr$refusals[[1]]$message
#> [1] "spending limit reached: the 'reduce' request could cost up to $0.01 (up to 232 prompt tokens, and 1500 reply tokens at its cap), and the run has spent $0.0024 of its $0.01 limit, so it was not sent; raise hr_options(max_cost_usd =) or ask for a smaller max_output"

The bound assumes two things harnessr cannot see. The provider must stop each reply at its cap, and its count of the prompt must fall within safety_margin of the local tokenizer’s.

A run that leaves its output caps at the model’s limit stops while it still has headroom that a smaller cap would have used. With the merge’s reply held to 500 tokens, the same run fits:

tr <- hr_trace(governor = hr_governor(max_cost_usd = 0.01))
fits <- gr_read(chunks, "What was revenue?", cl,
                gr_read_spec(reader = "map_reduce", model = "priced-mock",
                             max_answer_tokens = 500),
                trace = tr)
fits$partial
#> [1] FALSE
data.frame(calls = tr$calls, spent_usd = tr$spent_usd)
#>   calls spent_usd
#> 1     6  0.002922

A refused request is not a call, and it adds nothing to the trace’s calls, steps or spend. hr_call() first signals a condition of class hr_budget_refused, which you can catch to stop the run there. Otherwise it returns the request as a failed result with refused = TRUE and an error naming the limit. The trace lists the request in refusals, sets budget_stop and names the limit in stop_reason: "calls", "cost", "tokens", "output", "model" or "unpriced". Readers and review stages mark the answer or section partial and do not count the refused request as failed.

The check sits on the call path itself, so it covers every request: readers, judges, the ensemble’s adjudication, conflict resolution in gr_extract(), context and proposition segmentation, claims, outlines, screening, synthesis, embeddings, and any request a custom reader or a script makes with hr_call().

A governor for one run

hr_governor() holds a run’s six limits. Attach one with hr_trace(governor = ). A trace without a governor reads the limits from hr_options() at each check.

limit what it holds default
max_calls requests the run may make, cache hits and embeddings included 400
max_cost_usd what the run may spend, in USD 5
max_tokens_total tokens of every prompt, reply and embedded text off
max_output_tokens the largest output cap one request may carry; a request with a larger one is refused, not cut down off
allowed_models the model ids the run may call, text and embedding models alike any
allow_unpriced whether a model with no registered price may be called under a spending limit TRUE

Each limit is also an option of the same name: hr_options(max_tokens_total = 50000) sets it for every run, and each trace’s config snapshot lists all six. NULL or Inf removes a limit. A limit that cannot be compared is refused as soon as you set it:

tryCatch(hr_options(max_cost_usd = NA), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
#> [1] "hr_options(max_cost_usd = ) must be a single number or NULL, not NA. A limit that cannot be compared is not a limit, so this is refused here rather than ignored later."

A request to a model the run may not call is refused the same way as one over budget:

tr <- hr_trace(governor = hr_governor(allowed_models = "gpt-4o"))
res <- hr_call(cl, "What was revenue?", model = "priced-mock", trace = tr)
data.frame(refused = res$refused, stop_reason = tr$stop_reason)
#>   refused stop_reason
#> 1    TRUE       model

gr_read_many(), gr_claims(), gr_outline() and gr_synthesise() keep a trace of their own and fold it into the trace you pass them. Their requests are held to that trace’s governor, less what it has already spent and the tokens it has used. max_calls stays a limit per document and per stage. gr_compare() holds the whole comparison to max_cost_usd and max_tokens_total.

A reserve for the closing request

A reader that works in rounds answers in one last request. When the rounds use up the limit, that request is refused, and the rounds already paid for end with no answer. reserve_calls and reserve_usd hold part of max_calls and max_cost_usd back for such a request. An ordinary request is refused once it would reach into the reserve; a request sent with hr_call(closing = TRUE) may spend it. The readers mark their final request this way, such as the iterative reader’s final answer and the map_reduce reader’s last merge.

tr <- hr_trace(governor = hr_governor(max_calls = 3, reserve_calls = 1))
rounds <- vapply(1:3, function(i) hr_call(cl, "Read on.", trace = tr)$ok, logical(1))
answer <- hr_call(cl, "Answer now.", trace = tr, closing = TRUE)
c(rounds = rounds, answer = answer$ok)
#> rounds1 rounds2 rounds3  answer 
#>    TRUE    TRUE   FALSE    TRUE
tr$refusals[[1]]$message
#> [1] "call cap reached: the run has made 2 of the 3 calls it may make, with 1 kept for closing requests, so the 'call' request was not sent; raise hr_options(max_calls =) or lower reserve_calls"

The third round was refused, so the answer had its call. Both reserves default to 0, which holds nothing back and leaves every request as it was. A reserve larger than its limit is refused with class hr_bad_reserve.

Models with no price

harnessr ships no prices, so a model has none until you set it. A language model with no price adds nothing to the spend, so the spending limit cannot hold it. Under max_cost_usd, a request to such a model is still sent: the trace prices it NA, never 0, and the first request to each such model in a session warns with class hr_unpriced_model. max_calls and max_tokens_total still count the request. allow_unpriced = FALSE, in hr_options() or hr_governor(), refuses it instead, with stop_reason "unpriced".

vignette("models") shows how to set prices for one model or many, runs both cases, and covers the warning harnessr gives when the prices you set grow old.

Parallel batches

With parallel = TRUE, per-chunk requests go out in batches that cannot be stopped part way. The limits apply to them like this:

  • Each worker’s items are held to an equal share of the calls and dollars the run has left.
  • An item that its worker’s share refuses before it is sent runs again in the calling process, against the run’s own limits.
  • A batch the run’s limits cannot cover runs in the calling process instead of being split across workers.
  • Batch items make one request each. An item that made more, and had a later one refused by its share, warns with class gr_parallel_share, and the run is not marked as stopped.

Paying once

hr_cache() stores each successful response, keyed on the exact request. A repeat is free and identical:

cache  <- hr_cache(file.path(tempdir(), "harnessr-runs-cache"))
cached <- hr_cache_client(cl, cache)

first  <- answer_document(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", "thorough",
                          client = cached, model = "priced-mock")
second <- answer_document(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", "thorough",
                          client = cached, model = "priced-mock")

hr_trace_summary(second$trace)[, c("calls", "cached", "tokens_in")]
#>   calls cached tokens_in
#> 1     1      1       607
hr_trace_cost(second$trace)[, c("calls", "paid_calls", "usd")]
#>   calls paid_calls usd
#> 1     1          0   0

cached counts the calls answered from the cache instead of the network, so calls - cached is what the run paid for. The token counts stay, since they show how big the prompts were. A run with cached == calls cost nothing, though, so do not pass its totals to hr_estimate_cost() and call the result a bill.

The key covers everything that can change the reply: the messages, the model, the resolved output cap, the temperature, the reasoning effort, the JSON schema, any extra body fields, the API shape and the base URL. It leaves out the API key, the headers, the timeout and the retry policy, since the model sees none of them. If a header changes which model answers, give that client its own base_url or model so the cache can tell the two apart.

These replies are never cached, so running again asks again:

  • failures: a rate limit or a refusal belongs to the moment, and storing one would make a blip permanent;
  • a reply cut off at its output cap;
  • a structured reply that does not fit its schema, when the readers or ctx$call_json() in a benchmark arm make the request. hr_call() does not parse a reply, so it caches a reply to a schema call like any other (see vignette("core")).

The default directory is under tempdir(), so a cache costs nothing and vanishes with the session. For a long run, point it at a lasting directory to make the run resumable. After a crash, a restart gets every completed call from the cache instead of paying for it again:

hr_options(cache_dir = tools::R_user_dir("harnessr", "cache"))

hr_cache_stats() reports entries, bytes, hits, misses and writes, and hr_cache_clear() empties a cache. Set write = FALSE to run against a frozen cache, or read = FALSE to refresh entries already stored.

Repeated draws

At a temperature above zero, a cache hit replays one sample instead of drawing a new one. That makes a run reproducible. It also turns N identical calls into one draw repeated N times, so any check that compares them sees perfect agreement. To keep N draws, give each call its own draw_index. An index above 0 is part of the key, so draws 1 to N are N entries, and a rerun gets the same N replies back in the same order:

n <- 0
sampler <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) { n <<- n + 1; paste("draw", n) })
sampler <- hr_cache_client(sampler, hr_cache(file.path(tempdir(), "harnessr-runs-draws")))

vapply(1:3, function(k) hr_call(sampler, "Pick one.", draw_index = k)$text, "")
#> [1] "draw 1" "draw 2" "draw 3"
vapply(1:3, function(k) hr_call(sampler, "Pick one.", draw_index = k)$text, "")
#> [1] "draw 1" "draw 2" "draw 3"

The cache answers the second line. A call with the default draw_index = 0 keys as an ordinary call always has. For new replies to draws already stored, use a fresh directory or read = FALSE.

Older caches

Entries are keyed by a SHA-256 hash under harnessr-cache-v3. Calls with no draw index still read entries written under the old key, readgpt-cache-v2, by readgpt 0.6.0 and earlier builds of harnessr. The first reply found that way in a session warns once, with class hr_legacy_key, and hr_cache_stats() counts these replies as legacy_hits. Old entries are never rewritten, and hr_cache_clear() removes both kinds. With tools::R_user_dir("harnessr", "cache") set, entries readgpt kept in tools::R_user_dir("readgpt", "cache") are read too, after it.

Replaying a run

A trace records every prompt and every response, which makes it a complete transcript of the only non-deterministic part of the pipeline. A trace plus the source document reproduces a run exactly, with no key and no spend:

f <- file.path(tempdir(), "run.json")
hr_trace_save(first$trace, f)

replayed <- answer_document(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", "thorough",
                            client = hr_replay_client(f), model = "priced-mock")
identical(replayed$answer, first$answer)
#> [1] TRUE

Publish the trace with the paper, and a reader can reproduce the run instead of paying to approximate it. A trace file also makes a bug report you can run again, since it records exactly what went wrong.

A replay matches each reply on the key harnessr-replay-v2, which each step records as replay_key. The key covers:

  • the prompt messages;
  • the model the call asked for, and its effort;
  • its temperature, once the session default is filled in;
  • the output cap asked for, and its JSON schema.

A prompt with no recorded reply raises gr_replay_miss rather than getting an invented answer. A miss means the replay has diverged from the recording, and a result that looks like the original but differs from it is worse than no replay at all. If the prompt was recorded under other settings, the error message names the recorded temperature, cap or schema next to the ones asked for. Pass strict = FALSE to run a partial recording anyway.

Asking a replay for more replies than were recorded is an error too, of class hr_replay_exhausted. Draw k of a request gets the reply recorded for that draw:

tr <- hr_trace()
n <- 0
sampler <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) { n <<- n + 1; paste("draw", n) })
invisible(lapply(1:3, function(k) hr_call(sampler, "Pick one.", draw_index = k, trace = tr)))

rp <- hr_replay_client(tr)
vapply(1:3, function(k) hr_call(rp, "Pick one.", draw_index = k)$text, "")
#> [1] "draw 1" "draw 2" "draw 3"
tryCatch(hr_call(rp, "Pick one.", draw_index = 4),
         hr_replay_exhausted = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
#> [1] "The recording holds no reply for draw 4 of this request; it holds 3 draw(s) of it. The replay is making more calls than the recorded run did, so it is not reproducing that run. Pass on_exhausted = \"flag\" to hr_replay_client() to repeat the last recorded reply instead, counted in $stats()$repeats."

hr_replay_client(on_exhausted = "flag") repeats the last recorded reply instead, as every replay did before, and counts each repeat in $stats()$repeats. A step recorded before replay_key existed is looked up by the old key, readgpt-replay-v1, which covers messages, model and effort only. Such a lookup warns with hr_legacy_key once per recording in a session.

Embeddings in a replay

A trace records each embeddings request and its cost. It does not keep the vectors that came back. A replay reproduces a run’s chunk ranking exactly only when the recording used a deterministic embedder and the replay uses the same one. Both conditions must hold: a replay of an API-embedded run with a deterministic local embedder would compute vectors the original never saw, and the result would look exact.

In any other case the replay warns (gr_replay_no_embeddings) and falls back to lexical vectors. Lexical vectors place semantic cuts and rank chunks differently, so a replay of a run that used embeddings (the needle recipe, the retrieve and iterative readers, the semantic segmenter) usually sends prompts the recording does not hold. A strict replay then stops with gr_replay_miss, and the error message names this cause.

Record a run you intend to publish with hr_options(embedder = "lexical"), as this guide does, or with your own embedder registered as deterministic = TRUE:

run <- answer_document(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", "needle",
                       client = cl, model = "priced-mock")
again <- answer_document(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", "needle",
                         client = hr_replay_client(run$trace), model = "priced-mock")
identical(again$chunks_used, run$chunks_used)
#> [1] TRUE

Limits in a replay

A saved trace records whether a limit cut the run short, in budget_stop and stop_reason. A replay under the limits the run was recorded with stops at the same point. Replayed calls count against max_calls as they did when recorded.

Spend depends on how the recorded run ended. If the spending limit stopped it, each replayed call counts its recorded cost against max_cost_usd, in the trace’s replayed_usd, though nothing is spent. For any other run, replayed calls count nothing against it, so the replaying session’s limit does not stop a replay of an expensive run. A replay under a higher limit that asks for a call past the recorded stop gets a gr_replay_miss that says so.

A trace keeps only a hash of the JSON schema a call requested, in the step’s key. In a recording made before replay_key existed, two calls that differ only by schema, temperature or output cap share a reply.

Comparing what recipes cost

gr_compare() runs several recipes over one document on one trace. Its summary has a row per recipe with what the recipe cost:

  • calls, tokens_in and tokens_out;
  • usd, priced at each model’s registered price;
  • usd_estimated, the share of those dollars spent on requests whose token counts were estimated locally.

Pass correct, either strings a right answer contains or a function of each answer, and the summary gains correct and usd_per_correct, the cost of a right answer:

cmp <- gr_compare(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", c("fast", "precise", "thorough"),
                  client = cl, model = "priced-mock", correct = "45.2 million")
cmp$summary[, c("recipe", "reader", "calls", "usd", "usd_estimated",
                "correct", "usd_per_correct")]
#>     recipe     reader calls      usd usd_estimated correct usd_per_correct
#> 1     fast      stuff     1 0.001318             1    TRUE        0.001318
#> 2  precise       skim     3 0.001998             1    TRUE        0.001998
#> 3 thorough map_reduce     1 0.001318             1    TRUE        0.001318

usd_per_correct is usd for a right answer, Inf for a wrong one that cost something, and NA when correctness is not known. A recipe that a limit stopped before it found anything is NA, not wrong. Each recipe is charged for a segmentation it shares with an earlier recipe, as if it ran alone, so the usd column can add up to more than hr_trace_cost(cmp$trace).

Choosing the settings

Two walkthroughs cover the settings that hold a run in: the limits every run has, and the governor a benchmark or a batch shares. Each gives what the setting controls and what it trades off, the signs in your results that point to changing it, where its default came from, and how to test a change. effort_mode, effort that rises only when a stage needs it, has its walkthrough in vignette("effort"). vignette("settings") lists every option with its default.

The global limits

What they control. max_cost_usd and max_calls hold every run, and max_tokens_total, max_output_tokens, allowed_models and allow_unpriced hold it further when set (see “Limits” above). reserve_calls and reserve_usd keep part of the first two for a run’s closing request (see “A reserve for the closing request”). A limit set too low ends runs early, with partial answers. One set too high lets a mistake run up its full cost, such as a reader that sends every chunk of a long document at a small chunk size.

Signs they need changing. Any of these means a limit stopped the run:

  • an answer with partial = TRUE and cost_cap_reached or call_cap_reached in its notes;
  • a trace whose stop_reason is set;
  • an error of class gr_call_cap or gr_cost_cap before the first request.

Raise the limit only after checking that the run should cost that much. hr_estimate_cost() and gr_chunk_stats() tell you before anything is sent. If a run spends far less than its limit every time, you can lower the limit to catch the run that does not. A refusal with stop_reason = "output" means a request’s output cap was larger than max_output_tokens allows. Lower the reader’s caps (max_answer_tokens, max_chunk_tokens) to fit it.

Where the defaults came from. $5 and 400 calls are limits for one read, chosen so a mistake costs little. No measurement backs them, and gr_settings_table("options") declares no evidence for them. The other limits are off by default. allow_unpriced is TRUE because harnessr ships no prices: FALSE would refuse every request to a built-in model until you set its prices. Set it to FALSE when every request must count against the spending limit. The reserves are 0, so nothing is held back unless you ask; untested, a choice rather than a tuned value. Set reserve_calls = 1 when a run that works in rounds ends with no answer and stop_reason set.

How to test them. A limit belongs to the run, not to an arm, so a sweep can only test which settings fit under it. A reader’s output caps decide how much of the limit each request reserves, so sweep the merge’s cap and hold each arm’s five runs to the same $0.02:

qa <- gr_qa_reference(questions = c(revenue = "What was revenue in 2024?"),
                      documents = gr_example(), answers = list("45.2 million"),
                      split = "dev")
arms <- hr_sweep(gr_arm("thorough", list(method = "sentence", max_tokens = 150,
                                         overlap_tokens = 0, model = "priced-mock")),
                 list(max_answer_tokens = c(1500, 500)))
vapply(arms, function(arm) {
  b <- suppressWarnings(hr_benchmark(arm, qa, runs = 5, client = cl, split = "dev",
                                     scorer = gr_scorer_answer(),
                                     governor = hr_governor(max_cost_usd = 0.02)))
  c(stopped = sum(b$failure_kind %in% "budget_stop"), usd = sum(b$usd))
}, numeric(2))
#>         thorough:max_answer_tokens=1500 thorough:max_answer_tokens=500
#> stopped                        3.000000                        0.00000
#> usd                            0.013344                        0.01485

With the merge’s reply capped at 1500 tokens, each merge reserves $0.012 of output, so 3 of the 5 runs were stopped before their merge. Capped at 500, all five finished within the same limit. suppressWarnings() hides the hr_budget_stopped warning each benchmark gives; read it in your own runs.

The governor of a benchmark or a batch

What it controls. hr_governor() holds limits for more than one run. hr_benchmark(governor = ) holds the whole benchmark to it, and each run to what the runs before it left. gr_read_many() and the review stages hold their documents to the governor of the trace you pass them. A governor sized too small refuses the last arms or documents. One sized too large lets a mistake in one arm spend the budget meant for all of them.

Signs it needs changing. hr_benchmark() warns with class hr_budget_stopped, naming how many runs were stopped and by which limit, and the stopped runs have failure_kind = "budget_stop". If arms late in the list stopped more than early ones, suspect a governor too small for the whole benchmark rather than an arm that costs too much.

Where the default came from. governor = NULL takes the limits from hr_options() when the benchmark starts. Those are set for one read (400 calls), and a benchmark of two arms on 300 items for 5 runs needs several thousand. Size the governor for the benchmark: arms x items x runs x requests per run.

How to test it. Count the requests one run makes, multiply, and check how much of the governor was used:

per_run <- 6  # map_reduce over five chunks: five chunk requests and a merge
needed <- length(arms) * 1 * 5 * per_run
bench <- hr_benchmark(arms, qa, runs = 5, client = cl, split = "dev",
                      scorer = gr_scorer_answer(),
                      governor = hr_governor(max_calls = needed, max_cost_usd = 1))
c(allowed = needed, used = attr(bench, "trace")$calls,
  stopped = sum(bench$failure_kind %in% "budget_stop"))
#> allowed    used stopped 
#>      60      60       0

vignette("compare") sizes a governor this way for every benchmark it runs.
